title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Restore Former Rule 123D
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Restore Former Rule 123D

1. Purpose New York Stock Exchange LLC (``NYSE'' or the ``Exchange'') proposes restore former Rule 123D to its rulebook and mark it ``Reserved.'' In July 2025, the Exchange proposed to reorganize its trading halt rules into Rule 7.18 and to delete Rule 123D, where some trading halt rules had been located. That filing proposed to delete Rule 123D in its entirety, completely removing any reference to it from the Exchange's rulebook. The Commission noticed the proposed rule change for immediate effectiveness, and the change became operative in August 2026 in a coordinated roll-out of trading halt changes with other equities exchanges. For the sake of posterity, the Exchange now wishes to add former Rule 123D back into its rulebook and note that the rule is ``Reserved.'' In so doing, the Exchange would also add back the adoption and amendment history of Rule 123D, so that the history and legacy of the rule and its development is preserved in the rulebook. The proposed change is non-substantive. The content of former Rule 123D would remain deleted; this filing would only restore its title, the word ``Reserved,'' and its adoption and amendment history. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder that are applicable to a national securities exchange, and, in particular, with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act. Specifically, the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act because it would promote just and equitable principles of trade, remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would protect investors and the public interest and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system. Adding reference to former Rule 123D back into the rulebook as ``Reserved'' and restoring its adoption and amendment history would preserve the legacy of the rule and its development, thereby providing clarity and transparency for the Exchange and for market participants about the rule's history and evolution. B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition The Exchange believes the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act in that it does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act as explained below. Rather than impacting competition, the proposed change would simply add back into the Exchange's rulebook the title ``Rule 123D,'' the word ``Reserved,'' and the former rule's adoption and amendment history. C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change. III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder. Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b- 4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder. A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6) normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii), the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposal may become operative immediately upon filing with the Commission pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and paragraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder. The Commission believes that it is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest to waive the operative date of the proposal so that it becomes operative upon filing. The Commission believes that the waiver would provide member organizations greater clarity about the recent changes to the Exchange's trading halt rules. In addition, the proposal does not present any unique or novel regulatory issues because it simply adds back into the Exchange's rulebook the title ``Rule 123D,'' the word ``reserved,'' and the ``former rule's adoption and amendment history.'' For this reason, the Commission hereby waives the 30-day operative period and designates the proposal operative upon filing. At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B) of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved. IV. Solicitation of Comments Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods: Electronic Comments Use the Commission's internet comment form (https://www.sec.gov/rules/sro.shtml); or Send an email to [email protected]. Please include file number SR-NYSE-2026-49 on the subject line. Paper Comments Send paper comments in triplicate to Secr

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Texas Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Adopt Corporate Listing Fees on the Exchange
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Texas Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Adopt Corporate Listing Fees on the Exchange

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to add Section G to its Fee Schedule to establish an initial corporate listing fee framework for securities listed pursuant to Chapter 16 of the TXSE Rules. The proposed section would establish an Entry Fee, an Initial Application Fee, and All-Inclusive Annual Listing Fees, including a separate annual fee for Companies with Dually-Listed Securities. The proposal also specifies the timing of assessments, transfer exemptions, fee-credit mechanics, proration, and limited circumstances in which fees may be deferred or waived. Entry Fee A Company would pay a one-time Entry Fee of $325,000 the first time it lists any class of securities on the Exchange. The fee would be assessed on the date of listing. A Company whose business plan is to complete one or more acquisitions (an ``Acquisition Company'' or ``SPAC'') would instead pay a flat $80,000 Entry Fee. That fee would cover the SPAC's primary equity securities and any units, warrants, or rights issued in connection with the listing. The lower SPAC Entry Fee recognizes that a SPAC generally lists a package of related securities at the same time and has not yet completed a Business Combination. A Company transferring the listing of any class of equity securities from another national securities exchange would not pay an Entry Fee. The transfer exemption is designed to reduce duplicative costs for an issuer that has already completed an exchange listing process and to support competition among listing markets. The Exchange Board or its designee may, in its discretion, defer or waive all or any portion of an Entry Fee. Any exercise of that authority would be administered in a manner consistent with the Exchange Act, including the requirements that exchange fees be equitably allocated and not unfairly discriminatory. Initial Application Fee A Company, including a SPAC, would pay a non-refundable Initial Application Fee of $25,000 in connection with its first application to list an equity security on the Exchange. The Exchange would not grant eligibility clearance until it receives the Initial Application Fee. If the Company lists, the Initial Application Fee would be credited in full toward the applicable Entry Fee, so the fee would not increase the total Entry Fee paid by a successful first-time applicant. A Company transferring the listing of any class of equity securities from another national securities exchange would be exempt from the Initial Application Fee. In addition, a Company that pays the Initial Application Fee but does not immediately list would not pay a second Initial Application Fee upon a later listing if it continues to have a registration statement regarding the security on file with the Commission or, after withdrawing the registration statement, refiles it within 24 months. These provisions avoid duplicative charges where the Exchange can continue to rely on the application work associated with the earlier submission. All-Inclusive Annual Listing Fees A Company would pay All-Inclusive Annual Fees for the continued listing of its securities. In the first year of listing, the Exchange would assess a prorated fee covering the period from the listing date through the end of the calendar year. For each later year, the Exchange would invoice the applicable annual fee at the beginning of the year. A Company transferring its primary class of shares or units from another national securities exchange would not pay the All-Inclusive Annual Fee for that primary class for the transfer year. The exemption recognizes that a transferring Company may already have paid an annual listing fee to its prior exchange. Except as expressly provided in the Fee Schedule, an annual fee that is due and payable would not be waived or refunded if a class is later delisted or otherwise removed. The Exchange Board or its designee may defer or waive all or any portion of an All-Inclusive Annual Fee, subject to the Exchange Act requirements described above. Primary Listed Securities For primary listed securities, the All-Inclusive Annual Fee for each class would equal the greater of the applicable minimum fee or the number of shares outstanding as of December 31 of the preceding year multiplied by $0.001250 per share, subject to a $250,000 maximum. The applicable minimum would be $70,000 for common shares and for a primary class of preferred stock where no common shares are listed, and $15,000 for each other class of preferred stock and each class of warrants, units, or rights. Additional common-share and preferred-stock issuances during the year of issuance would not generate an additional fee. The per-share design, minimum fees, and maximum fee are intended to allocate annual fees in relation to the scale of the listed class while providing Companies with a predictable floor and ceiling. This structure is similar to the per-share annual fee schedules used by other national securities exchanges. As an example, a Company with 40 million common shares outstanding would pay the $70,000 minimum because 40 million multiplied by $0.001250 equals $50,000. A Company with 100 million common shares outstanding would pay $125,000. A Company with 300 million common shares outstanding would pay the $250,000 maximum because the calculated amount would otherwise equal $375,000. Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 7.10 (Clearly Erroneous Executions)

1. Purpose The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend Rule 7.10 (Clearly Erroneous Executions). Specifically, the Exchange proposes to: (1) reorganize the Rule to enhance its clarity; (2) specify the impact of missing or erroneous LULD Price Bands on the availability of Clearly Erroneous review during the Core Trading Session or Overnight Protected Hours; (3) amend provisions on ``multi-stock events''; (4) remove references to ``multi-day events''; (5) add a provision on reasonable cross-market coordination; and (6) eliminate redundancies in the Rule. Background Following a severe disruption in the U.S. equities markets on May 6, 2010 (known as the Flash Crash), the Commission approved, on a pilot basis, the clearly erroneous rule to ``provide greater transparency and certainty to the process of breaking trades.'' Largely, the pilot reduced the discretion of the Exchange, other national securities exchanges, and Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (``FINRA'') to deviate from the objective standards in their respective rules when dealing with potentially erroneous transactions. After revisions in 2013 and 2014, the clearly erroneous pilot was extended in six-month increments numerous times until 2022. In April 2019, the Commission approved an amendment to the LULD Plan to make that Plan permanent. Following that change, in 2022, the Commission approved a proposal to amend the clearly erroneous rule (the ``2022 Amendment'' to Rule 7.10). The 2022 Amendment made the clearly erroneous rule permanent and aimed to harmonize it with the LULD Plan by making explicit that, with limited exceptions, the LULD mechanism was the primary means of preventing clearly erroneous trades during the Core Trading Session. In 2026, in conjunction with the industry's plans for the introduction of 23/5 Trading, the Operating Committee of the LULD Plan filed proposed Amendment 27 to the LULD Plan, which proposed to establish price band protections during overnight trading hours (``Overnight Price Bands''). On August 5, 2026, the Commission approved the proposal. On September 14, 2026, in light of the addition of Overnight Price Bands to the LULD Plan, the Exchange filed an amendment to Rule 7.10 that extended the restrictions on clearly erroneous review that apply in the Core Trading Session to the Overnight Protected Hours when Overnight Price Bands are in place. Proposed Amendment Following the 2022 Amendment, market disruptions on January 24, 2023 and June 3, 2024 further highlighted the close interplay of the LULD Plan and the clearly erroneous rule. Following those events, the Exchange, in consultation with other equities exchanges, closely reviewed the current text of Rule 7.10 and identified areas where the Exchange believes the Rule's clarity can be enhanced, its organization can be improved, and duplicate and obsolete sections can be eliminated. In sum, the proposed rule text is not substantively new, but rather a reorganization and further specification of existing Exchange authority. Accordingly, the Exchange proposes to reorganize Rule 7.10 into three clear paragraphs: (a) Definitions, (b) Availability of Clearly Erroneous Review, and (c) Procedures. In the current Rule, definitions are spread across paragraphs (a), (c), and (d); rules on the availability of clearly erroneous review are split between paragraphs (c), (g), (h), and (i); and procedures are split across paragraphs (b), (c), (e), and (f). By reorganizing the Rule and gathering similar provisions together, the Exchange believes the proposed rule text will be easier for market participants to navigate, understand, and use. (a) Definitions The Exchange proposes to amend paragraph (a) of Rule 7.10 to include the definitions of terms used in the current version of the Rule, as well as new terms that would be added as a result of this proposal, as follows: Proposed paragraph (a) would be titled ``Definitions'' and would provide that ``[f]or purposes of this Rule, the terms below have the following meanings.'' Proposed subparagraph (a)(1) would define ``CEE Reference Price'' as the consolidated last sale immediately prior to the execution(s) under review, or, in cases where there are no prior trades, the previous day's official closing price, unless an Officer determines to utilize a Revised CEE Reference Price as provided in this Rule. The first part of this definition is based on the current definition of ``Reference Price'' in paragraph (d) of Rule 7.10. The second part of this definition is based on the Exchange's definition of ``Official Closing Price'' in Rule 1.1(u)(1)(D), which states that when there have been no consolidated last-sale eligible trades during the Core Trading Hours on that trading day, the Exchange's Official Closing Price will be the previous day's Official Closing Price. As such, the proposed definition of ``CEE Reference Price'' in subparagraph (a)(1) is not novel. Proposed subparagraph (a)(2), the definition of ``Clearly erroneous,'' would encompass the text of current paragraph (a), without substantive change. Proposed subparagraph (a)(3) would define ``LULD Plan'' to mean the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility Pursuant to Rule 608 of Regulation NMS under the Act. This term is currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10. Proposed subparagraph (a)(4) would define ``LULD Price Bands'' or ``Price Bands'' as the Price Bands defined in Section V of the LULD Plan and Overnight Price Bands as defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. These terms are currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10. Proposed subparagraph (a)(5) would define ``LULD Protected Hours'' to include the Core Trading Session and Overnight Protected Hours. This term is currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10. Proposed subparagraph (a)(6) would define ``LULD Reference Price'' as the Reference Price or Overnight Reference Prices defined in the LULD Plan. Self-Regulatory Organizations; The Options Clearing Corporation; Notice of Filing of Proposed Rule Change by The Options Clearing Corporation Concerning Revisions to OCC Rule 213-Cybersecurity Obligations

1. Purpose OCC's proposed amendments to Rule 213 are intended to further promote resiliency, strengthen OCC's cybersecurity protocols, and maintain consistency with industry standards, including by aligning OCC's Rules with recent rule amendments of similarly situated self- regulatory organizations (``SROs'') with overlapping membership with OCC. Among other things, OCC's proposed enhancements to Rule 213 would: Add a defined terms section to Rule 213, including defining OCC's ``Systems'' to include not only direct connections, but also established communication channels (e.g., access to File Transfer Protocols (``FTPs'') for transmitting data or instructions that may be compromised by a systems intrusion to a Clearing Member's back-office systems); Require the Cybersecurity Confirmation to be signed by a senior executive of the Clearing Member or applicant who is authorized to attest to such matters; Remove language that invites a Clearing Member to assess the potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems and operations when determining whether such incident is reportable, specify the timeframe in which OCC requires a Clearing Member System Event to be reported, and identify the specific information a Clearing Member must include in such notice; Establish the concept of a ``Major Clearing Member System Event,'' including a declaration requiring the approval of two or more Designated Officers and prompt notification to the Chairman of the Board of Directors; Reorganize and clarify OCC's authority to take action in response to a Clearing Member System Event, including specifying the actions that constitute a ``disconnect,'' and clarify a Clearing Member's related cooperation obligations; Add provisions incorporating the reporting, testing, and approval requirements, process, obligations, and governance necessary for reconnection, including the ability for OCC to require an audit report from a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm; and Provide OCC with the authority to inform, or require the Clearing Member to inform, the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider of the Clearing Member System Event if OCC determines, in its discretion, that such action is necessary for the protection of OCC and other Clearing Members. As described in more detail below, OCC believes its proposed changes will strengthen OCC's security protocols by enhancing Rule 213 to be more efficient, effective and clear in its cybersecurity obligations of Clearing Members so that OCC may better address cybersecurity risks to protect OCC and its Clearing Members. Furthermore, OCC believes its proposed changes will enable OCC's Clearing Members to better understand and prepare for their obligations to OCC as it relates to a cybersecurity event. Proposed Changes Proposed Rule 213(a) --Defined Terms First, OCC proposes to introduce new section (a) titled ``Defined Terms.'' To strengthen the provisions of proposed Rule 213 and further clarify OCC's requirements related to the cybersecurity obligations of a Clearing Member, OCC proposes to define several terms specifically for the purposes of Rule 213. OCC's proposed changes would: Define ``Best Practices'' to mean policies, procedures, practices or similar standards and guidelines that are reasonably designed and consistent with then current financial-sector cybersecurity standards issued by an authoritative body that is a U.S. governmental entity or agency, an association of a U.S. governmental entity or agency, or a widely recognized industry organization. The purpose of defining ``Best Practices'' is to clarify the standards that OCC would require a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm to employ when such firm is engaged, as would be required by OCC Rule 213 as discussed further below. OCC's proposed definition of ``Best Practices'' aligns with Section 1001(a)(4) of the Commission's Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (``Reg SCI''). Delete OCC's existing definition of a ``Security Incident'' and replace it with ``Clearing Member System Event.'' OCC proposes to define a ``Clearing Member System Event'' to mean an incident resulting from the unintended or unauthorized access to, or the malfunction or corruption (whether partial or total) of one or more systems, of a Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider, connected to OCC's Systems. The purpose of re-defining the concept of a ``Security Incident'' to a ``Clearing Member System Event'' is to capture only those disruptions to systems connected to OCC's Systems, whether via an established communication channel from a Clearing Member, or through the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider; it is not intended to capture every disruption to every system of the Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider. In addition, as described in further detail in section (d) of proposed Rule 213, OCC proposes to eliminate the existing definition of a ``Security Incident'' to remove language that invites Clearing Members to assess the potential impact of such incident on OCC's Systems and operations when determining whether an incident is reportable. OCC's existing definition of a ``Security Incident,'' is defined, in part, as an incident, or an incident that is occurring, involving a cyber- related disruption or intrusion of the Clearing Member's systems that is reasonably likely to pose an imminent risk or threat to OCC's operations. OCC believes the language in the existing definition invites Clearing Members to assess whether such incident to their systems would impact OCC, and therefore OCC proposes to eliminate the definition of ``Security Incident'' and replace the definition with ``Clearing Member System Event'' in proposed Rule 213. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to modify the Fee Schedule to adjust the fees and rebates applicable to Manual transactions. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to (1) amend the fees applicable to Manual transactions in non-Penny issues executed by e-Specialists, Market Makers, and Specialists (collectively, ``Market Makers''), and (2) establish a rebate payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with a Market Maker order on the Trading Floor (``Trading Floor'' or ``Floor''). The Exchange proposes that these changes become effective October 14, 2026. With respect to the first proposed change, the Exchange proposes to amend Section I.A. of the Fee Schedule, which sets forth rates for Electronic and Manual transactions in both Penny and non-Penny issues. Currently, a $0.50 per contract fee applies to Market Makers' Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, except for those in MXEA, MXEF, MXUSA, MXWLD, and MXACW. The Exchange proposes to increase this fee to $0.90 per contract and then, effective November 1, 2026, increase the fee to $1.00 per contract. The increase to $1.00 per contract would align the Exchange's fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non- Penny issues consistent with similar fees adopted and proposed by other exchanges. The two-tiered increase is necessary to simplify the Exchange's billing process during the transition and to allow market participants sufficient time to adapt. The Exchange also proposes to establish a rebate of $0.20 per contract payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with Market Maker orders on the Trading Floor. For Floor Brokers that participate in the FB Prepay Program, the proposed rebate would apply in lieu of any rebates earned through the Manual Billable Rebate Program as provided in Section III.E. of the Fee Schedule. The Exchange proposes to add new text to Section III.E. of the Fee Schedule describing the proposed rebate. The Exchange believes that the proposed rebate for Penny and non- Penny issues would strengthen the Exchange's competitive position for order flow by incentivizing Floor Brokers to participate on the Trading Floor, including when the counterparty to such trading is a Market Maker, rather than routing such orders to other exchanges' trading floors. The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market for order flow, and Floor Brokers may readily direct their order flow to competing exchanges that offer more favorable pricing. Accordingly, the Exchange believes the proposed rebate is a reasonable means of remaining competitive and attracting order flow to its Trading Floor. The Exchange notes that, in August 2026, executions in non-Penny issues represented only 12% of executed Manual volume, underscoring that the proposed fee increase is much smaller in scope than the proposed Floor Broker rebate, which is applicable to executions in both Penny and non- Penny issues. Taken together with the proposed rebate payable to Floor Broker orders, the Exchange believes that the proposed increase in the Market Maker fee for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues from $0.50 to $0.90 per contract and then to $1.00 per contract beginning on November 1, 2026 would, on balance, not discourage Market Makers from continuing to participate in transactions on the Trading Floor, thereby promoting trading opportunities and competition on the Trading Floor to the benefit of all market participants. Specifically, the Exchange notes that Market Maker participation in non-Penny issues on the Trading Floor has continued to grow since the Exchange's initial fee increase on January 2, 2026. For example, in December 2025, prior to the Exchange's initial filing, Market Makers paid $0.50 per contract for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues and were involved in only 12% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. However, in August 2026, after the fee was raised to $1.00 per contract for Manual executions in non-Penny issues and, subsequently, to $0.90 per contract, Market Makers were involved in 20% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. Despite higher Market Maker fees for Manual transactions, the Exchange has continued to observe elevated Market Maker interest on the Trading Floor, even in non-Penny issues where the fee was specifically increased, demonstrating that this fee has not deterred, and will not deter Market Maker participation. The Exchange further notes that the amount of the proposed fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is within the range of fees currently in place for responses by Market Makers (and other market participants) in non-Penny issues in various electronic paired-order auction mechanisms on other options exchanges, which is largely analogous to the Manual transactions impacted by the proposed fee increase on the Trading Floor. For example, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (``EDGX'') imposes a $1.05 per contract fee on all market participants (including Market Makers) responding to Automated Improvement Mechanism Auctions (``AIM Auctions''), while charging the paired contra order only $0.02 per contract in non-Penny issues. In this example, the large disparity in fees between the auction responder and the paired contra order demonstrates the unique position of the responder to evaluate the full terms of a transaction immediately prior to execution, including size, pricing, and counterparty interest. This position enables responders to EDGX AIM Auctions to exercise discretion in determining whether to engage in a trade under informed conditions. In addition, the responder has a guaranteed participation entitlement of up to 60% of the trade under the relevant rules, even in the absence of price improvement. This allocation represents a meaningful structural advantage, as it ensures a substantial share of order flow once a responder elects to participate. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Its Fee Schedule To Update the Definition of Trading Platform
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Its Fee Schedule To Update the Definition of Trading Platform

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend the definition of ``Trading Platform'' set forth in the Definitions section of its Fee Schedule. The existing definition enumerates three categories of execution venue--a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, and an Electronic Communications Network. The Exchange now seeks to amend this definition to add a functional, use-based category--namely, any other system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity--so that the term also captures other systems that perform a functionally equivalent execution function. The amended definition identifies, as non-exhaustive examples, a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment. The current and proposed amended definitions are set forth below. Current Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), or an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS).'' Proposed Amended Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS), or any other system, facility, or platform (including but not limited to a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, or a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment) through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity.'' The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, including the increasing use of functionally equivalent execution systems that operate outside the three enumerated categories. For example, under the current definition, a platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, or an Electronic Communications Network plainly constitutes a Trading Platform and is thus subject to the applicable fees associated with a Trading Platform. However, a functionally equivalent system that performs the same execution function--such as a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow, or a decentralized or tokenized execution venue--is not expressly named in the current enumerated categories, despite performing the same execution function as the enumerated venues. To facilitate more consistent and equitable outcomes across functionally equivalent venues, the Exchange proposes to add this language so that ``Trading Platform'' better covers the intended scope of execution venues. The new framework operates as a functional, use-based standard. It reaches any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of the execution model employed. The definition expressly covers both (i) systems that match third-party orders against one another and (ii) systems in which the operator or its affiliate executes third-party orders in a principal trading capacity. Accordingly, a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/ or facilitates execution of client order flow falls within the definition on its face. The parenthetical examples--a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment--are illustrative only and the amended definition is not intended to limit the scope of the broader category. The requirement that orders be ``systematically executed by electronic means'' distinguishes covered systems from manual, negotiated, or voice-brokered bilateral trading. The amended definition is intended to capture emerging technologies and execution venues that are functionally analogous to venues with established regulatory definitions--including tokenized order books or decentralized execution protocols, to the extent they perform or support an execution function, and other novel platforms. These venues operate in a manner similar to defined legacy execution platforms and should be treated as such. The examples set out in the definition-- broker crossing systems not filed as ATSs, systematic internalization systems, and decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environments-- as well as the references to single-dealer platforms in this filing, are illustrative of this approach, not an exhaustive list, and the definition applies to any system through which third-party orders are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of label. The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity as to the scope of ``Trading Platform,'' with new and emerging execution technologies in mind. The Exchange notes that this update better aligns itself with the ongoing evolution of market structure and industry practice. 2. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 14.1 Regarding Information Circular Requirements
raw_text:
Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 14.1 Regarding Information Circular Requirements

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to: (1) amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rules 3.7 and 3.21; (2) eliminate the requirement that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Derivative Security that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange as provided in current Rule 14.1(c)(1) by deleting Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety; (3) amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities; (4) renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively; and (5) make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross- reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2). The proposal is based on Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (``BZX'') Rule 14.11(j). Rule 14.1(c) governs the trading of UTP Derivative Securities on the Exchange--securities listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (``UTP''). Under current Rule 14.1(c)(1), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Derivative Security that generally mirrors the information circular issued by the primary listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the Derivative Security; (b) the Exchange Rules that will apply to the Derivative Security, including Rule 3.7; (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indexes; and (d) the risk of trading during the Early Trading Session (7:00 a.m.--8:00 a.m. Eastern Time), Pre-Opening Session (8:00 a.m.--9:30 a.m. Eastern Time) and the Post-Closing Session (4:00 p.m.-- 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time) due to the lack of calculation or dissemination of the intra-day indicative value or a similar value. The Exchange proposes to delete Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety. The information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes. The Exchange's issuance of a separate, duplicative circular therefore serves no independent investor protection function. The existing Member-level suitability and customer disclosure obligations under Rules 3.7 and 3.21 continue to apply independently of the information circular requirement. The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rule 3.7 (Recommendations to Customers) and Rule 3.21 (Customer Disclosures). The Exchange is adding express cross- references to those rules in Rule 14.1(a) to enhance their visibility in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross- references are intended to make the applicable framework explicit in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. Rule 3.7 independently requires Members to ensure that any recommendation of a UTP Derivative Security is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, a standing obligation that applies regardless of whether the Exchange has issued a product-specific information circular. Similarly, Rule 3.21 independently requires Members, before accepting an order from a customer for execution in the Early Trading, Pre-Opening or Post-Closing Trading Session, to disclose to such customer that extended hours trading involves material trading risks, including the possibility of lower liquidity, high volatility, changing prices, unlinked markets, an exaggerated effect from news announcements, wider spreads and any other relevant risk, and this obligation is not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product- specific information circular. Because current Rule 14.1(c)(1) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange satisfies the notification obligation under current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B), deletion of Rule 14.1(c)(1) necessitates a conforming amendment to current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B). The Exchange proposes to amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Derivative Security, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the listing exchange's information circular in the same manner and to the same effect. Finally, the Exchange proposes to renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively, and to make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2). 2. 1. Purpose On August 30, 2011, the Exchange received approval of rules applicable to the qualification, listing and delisting of companies on the Exchange, which it modified on February 8, 2012 in order to adopt pricing for the listing of exchange-traded products (``ETPs'') on the Exchange. Effective January 1, 2019, the Exchange amended Rule 14.13 to adopt annual listing fees for ETPs, including a reduced annual listing fee of $4,000 for ETPs listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 (a ``Legacy Listing''). Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) now sets forth the annual listing fee structure for ETPs, which distinguishes among ETPs based on, among other things, the date on which an ETP first listed on the Exchange. The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) to eliminate the $4,000 annual listing fee currently applicable to Legacy Listings. Currently, Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) provides that the issuer of each class of securities (not otherwise identified in Rule 14.13) that is a domestic or foreign issue listed on the Exchange as an ETP shall pay an annual listing fee to the Exchange, and that an issuer will be charged the lowest applicable fee among the categories set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i) through (vi). Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i) currently provides: ``[w]here an ETP was listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 (a ``Legacy Listing'') or is a Transfer Listing, such ETP will have an annual listing fee of $4,000.'' Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) also provides for an annual listing fee of $4,500 for a New Listing; a collective maximum annual listing fee of $16,000 for a series of Outcome Strategy ETPs or a series of Defined Distribution Strategy ETPs; and an annual listing fee of $9,000 for an ADR Hedge. Under Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi), an ETP that is not a Legacy Listing, a New Listing, an Outcome Strategy ETP, a Defined Distribution Strategy ETP, an ADR Hedge, or a Transfer Listing is subject to an annual listing fee based on the consolidated average daily volume (``CADV'') of the ETP in the fourth quarter of the preceding calendar year, ranging from $5,000 for an ETP with CADV greater than 1,000,000 shares to $7,000 for an ETP with CADV of 0-10,000 shares. The Exchange proposes to delete the Legacy Listing category from Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i), such that the $4,000 annual listing fee would apply only to Transfer Listings. The Exchange also proposes to make a conforming change to Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi) to delete the reference to a Legacy Listing. As a result, an ETP listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 would no longer qualify for the $4,000 annual listing fee by virtue of its initial listing date, and would instead be charged the lowest applicable annual listing fee for which it otherwise qualifies under Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E), including the CADV-based fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi). The proposed rule change does not amend the annual listing fees applicable to Transfer Listings, New Listings, Outcome Strategy ETPs, Defined Distribution Strategy ETPs, or ADR Hedges, or the CADV-based fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi). The Legacy Listing category was designed to preserve a reduced annual listing fee for ETPs that were already listed on the Exchange when the Exchange adopted its current annual listing fee structure. More than seven years have passed since January 1, 2019, and the Exchange believes that it is no longer appropriate to differentiate the annual listing fee applicable to an ETP based solely on whether the ETP first listed on the Exchange before or after that date. Rather, the Exchange believes that all ETPs listed on the Exchange should be subject to the same objective criteria in determining the applicable annual listing fee, namely the characteristics of the product and its trading activity, as reflected in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(ii) through (vi). Transfer Listings would continue to be eligible for the $4,000 annual listing fee, as the Exchange continues to believe that such fee is an appropriate incentive for issuers to transfer the listing of existing ETPs to the Exchange. The Exchange will implement the proposed change beginning with the annual listing fees assessed for calendar year 2027. Unless otherwise specified, the Exchange assesses all annual fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2) upon initial listing and in the first quarter of the calendar year. Accordingly, the proposed change will not affect any annual listing fee already assessed for calendar year 2026, and affected issuers will have notice of the proposed change in advance of the assessment of annual listing fees for calendar year 2027. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that the proposed rule changes are consistent with the objectives of Section 6 of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5), in particular, as it is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among its issuers, and it does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers or dealers. The Exchange believes that the proposed elimination of the Legacy Listing category from Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) is reasonable because it will subject all ETPs listed on the Exchange to the same objective criteria for determining the applicable annual listing fee, based on the characteristics of the product and its trading activity, rather than on the date on which the ETP first listed on the Exchange. The Exchange believes that a distinction based solely on whether an ETP listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 is no longer warranted given the passage of time since the Exchange adopted its current annual listing fee structure. Further, the annual listing fees that will apply to former Legacy Listings are the same fees that currently apply to all other ETPs listed on the Exchange that are not Transfer Listings, which the Exchange believes remain reasonable. 1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to modify the Fee Schedule to adjust the fees and rebates applicable to Manual transactions. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to (1) amend the fees applicable to Manual transactions in non-Penny issues executed by LMMs and Market Makers (collectively, ``Market Makers''), and (2) establish a rebate payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with a Market Maker order on the Trading Floor (``Trading Floor'' or ``Floor''). The Exchange proposes that these changes become effective October 14, 2026. With respect to the first proposed change, the Exchange proposes to amend the Fee Schedule, which sets forth rates for Manual executions in both Penny and non-Penny issues. Currently, a $0.50 per contract fee applies to Market Makers' Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, except for those in MXEA, MXEF, MXUSA, MXWLD, and MXACW. The Exchange proposes to increase this fee to $0.90 per contract and then, effective November 1, 2026, increase the fee to $1.00 per contract. The increase to $1.00 per contract would align the Exchange's fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues consistent with similar fees adopted and proposed by other exchanges. The two-tiered increase is necessary to simplify the Exchange's billing process during the transition and to allow market participants sufficient time to adapt. The Exchange also proposes to establish a rebate of $0.20 per contract payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with Market Maker orders on the Trading Floor. For Floor Brokers that participate in the FB Prepay Program, the proposed rebate would apply in lieu of any rebates earned through the Manual Billable Rebate Program as provided in the Fee Schedule. The Exchange proposes to add new text describing this rebate to Endnote 17. The Exchange believes that the proposed rebate for Penny and non- Penny issues would strengthen the Exchange's competitive position for order flow by incentivizing Floor Brokers to participate on the Trading Floor, including when the counterparty to such trading is a Market Maker, rather than routing such orders to other exchanges' trading floors. The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market for order flow, and Floor Brokers may readily direct their order flow to competing exchanges that offer more favorable pricing. Accordingly, the Exchange believes the proposed rebate is a reasonable means of remaining competitive and attracting order flow to its Trading Floor. The Exchange notes that, in August 2026, executions in non-Penny issues represented only 35% of executed Manual volume, underscoring that the proposed fee increase is much smaller in scope than the proposed Floor Broker rebate, which is applicable to executions in both Penny and non- Penny issues. Taken together with the proposed rebate payable to Floor Broker orders, the Exchange believes that the proposed increase in the Market Maker fee for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues from $0.50 to $0.90 per contract and then to $1.00 per contract beginning on November 1, 2026 would, on balance, not discourage Market Makers from continuing to participate in transactions on the Trading Floor, thereby promoting trading opportunities and competition on the Trading Floor to the benefit of all market participants. Specifically, the Exchange notes that Market Maker participation in non-Penny issues on the Trading Floor has continued to grow since the Exchange's initial fee increase on January 2, 2026. For example, in December 2025, prior to the Exchange's initial filing, Market Makers paid $0.50 per contract for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues and were involved in only 18% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. However, in August 2026, after the fee was raised to $1.00 per contract for Manual executions in non-Penny issues and, subsequently, to $0.90 per contract, Market Makers were involved in 39% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. Despite higher Market Maker fees for Manual transactions, the Exchange has continued to observe elevated Market Maker interest on the Trading Floor, even in non-Penny issues where the fee was specifically increased, demonstrating that this fee has not deterred, and will not deter Market Maker participation. The Exchange further notes that the amount of the proposed fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is within the range of fees currently in place for responses by Market Makers (and other market participants) in non-Penny issues on another electronic paired-order auction mechanisms [sic] on other options exchanges [sic], which is largely analogous to the Manual transactions impacted by the proposed fee increase on the Trading Floor. (``EDGX'') imposes a $1.05 per contract fee on all market participants (including Market Makers) responding to Automated Improvement Mechanism Auctions (``AIM Auctions''), while charging the paired contra order only $0.02 per contract in non-Penny issues. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Its Fee Schedule To Update the Definition of Trading Platform

Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Its Fee Schedule To Update the Definition of Trading Platform

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend the definition of ``Trading Platform'' set forth in the Definitions section of its Fee Schedule. The existing definition enumerates three categories of execution venue--a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, and an Electronic Communications Network. The Exchange now seeks to amend this definition to add a functional, use-based category--namely, any other system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity--so that the term also captures other systems that perform a functionally equivalent execution function. The amended definition identifies, as non-exhaustive examples, a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment. The current and proposed amended definitions are set forth below. Current Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), or an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS).'' Proposed Amended Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS), or any other system, facility, or platform (including but not limited to a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, or a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment) through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity.'' The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, including the increasing use of functionally equivalent execution systems that operate outside the three enumerated categories. For example, under the current definition, a platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, or an Electronic Communications Network plainly constitutes a Trading Platform and is thus subject to the applicable fees associated with a Trading Platform. However, a functionally equivalent system that performs the same execution function--such as a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow, or a decentralized or tokenized execution venue--is not expressly named in the current enumerated categories, despite performing the same execution function as the enumerated venues. To facilitate more consistent and equitable outcomes across functionally equivalent venues, the Exchange proposes to add this language so that ``Trading Platform'' better covers the intended scope of execution venues. The new framework operates as a functional, use-based standard. It reaches any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of the execution model employed. The definition expressly covers both (i) systems that match third-party orders against one another and (ii) systems in which the operator or its affiliate executes third-party orders in a principal trading capacity. Accordingly, a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/ or facilitates execution of client order flow falls within the definition on its face. The parenthetical examples--a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment--are illustrative only and the amended definition is not intended to limit the scope of the broader category. The requirement that orders be ``systematically executed by electronic means'' distinguishes covered systems from manual, negotiated, or voice-brokered bilateral trading. The amended definition is intended to capture emerging technologies and execution venues that are functionally analogous to venues with established regulatory definitions--including tokenized order books or decentralized execution protocols, to the extent they perform or support an execution function, and other novel platforms. These venues operate in a manner similar to defined legacy execution platforms and should be treated as such. The examples set out in the definition-- broker crossing systems not filed as ATSs, systematic internalization systems, and decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environments-- as well as the references to single-dealer platforms in this filing, are illustrative of this approach, not an exhaustive list, and the definition applies to any system through which third-party orders are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of label. The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity as to the scope of ``Trading Platform,'' with new and emerging execution technologies in mind. The Exchange notes that this update better aligns itself with the ongoing evolution of market structure and industry practice. 2. The proposal is based on Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (``BZX'') Rule 14.11(j). Rule 14.1(c) governs the trading of UTP Derivative Securities on the Exchange--securities listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (``UTP''). Under current Rule 14.1(c)(1), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Derivative Security that generally mirrors the information circular issued by the primary listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the Derivative Security; (b) the Exchange Rules that will apply to the Derivative Security, including Rule 3.7; (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indexes; and (d) the risk of trading during the Early Trading Session (7:00 a.m.-8:00 a.m. Eastern Time), Pre-Opening Session (8:00 a.m.-9:30 a.m. Eastern Time) and the Post-Closing Session (4:00 p.m.- 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time) due to the lack of calculation or dissemination of the intra-day indicative value or a similar value. The Exchange proposes to delete Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety. The information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes. The Exchange's issuance of a separate, duplicative circular therefore serves no independent investor protection function. The existing Member-level suitability and customer disclosure obligations under Rules 3.7 and 3.21 continue to apply independently of the information circular requirement. The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rule 3.7 (Recommendations to Customers) and Rule 3.21 (Customer Disclosures). The Exchange is adding express cross- references to those rules in Rule 14.1(a) to enhance their visibility in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross- references are intended to make the applicable framework explicit in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. Rule 3.7 independently requires Members to ensure that any recommendation of a UTP Derivative Security is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, a standing obligation that applies regardless of whether the Exchange has issued a product-specific information circular. Similarly, Rule 3.21 independently requires Members to disclose to customers the material risks of extended hours trading before accepting an order from a customer for execution in the Early Trading, Pre-Opening or Post-Closing Trading Session, a standing obligation not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product- specific information circular. Because current Rule 14.1(c)(1) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange satisfies the notification obligation under current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B), deletion of Rule 14.1(c)(1) necessitates a conforming amendment to current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B). The Exchange proposes to amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Derivative Security, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the listing exchange's information circular in the same manner and to the same effect. Finally, the Exchange proposes to renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively, and to make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2). 2. title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; The Options Clearing Corporation; Order Approving Proposed Rule Change by The Options Clearing Corporation Concerning Amendments to Clearing Member Standards

Self-Regulatory Organizations; The Options Clearing Corporation; Order Approving Proposed Rule Change by The Options Clearing Corporation Concerning Amendments to Clearing Member Standards

I. Introduction On August 19, 2026, the Options Clearing Corporation (``OCC'') filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (``Commission''), pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (``Exchange Act'') and Rule 19b-4 thereunder, a proposed rule change to amend OCC's requirements and procedures for membership as well as protective measures and sanctions including, but not limited to, the suspension of members (hereinafter ``Proposed Rule Change''). The Proposed Rule Change was published for comment in the Federal Register on September 8, 2026. The Commission received comments from interested persons. For the reasons discussed below, the Commission is approving the Proposed Rule Change. II. Background OCC is a central counterparty (``CCP''), which means that, as part of its function as a clearing agency, it interposes itself as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer for financial transactions. As the CCP for the listed options markets in the United States, as well as for certain futures and stock loans, OCC is exposed to various risks arising from providing clearance and settlement services to its Clearing Members because OCC is obligated to perform on the contracts it clears. OCC mitigates such risks, in part, by setting requirements for its members (and applicants to become members), the protective measures OCC may impose to manage specific risks, and the sanctions OCC may impose where members do not comply with the requirements of membership. Generally, the proposed changes affect OCC's requirements and procedures for membership as well as protective measures and sanctions including, but not limited to, the suspension of members. The proposed changes related to membership include conditions for admission of clearing member applicants as well as standards for existing Clearing Members. The proposed changes also include the adoption of several new definitions, technical, clarifying changes, amendments to OCC's governance standards, and, generally, the adoption of new rules relating to risk mitigation practices. A. Clearing Membership As noted above, OCC proposes changes to its membership rules. The proposed changes would address the conditions for admission of clearing member applicants as well as the who are authorized to approve or deny such applications. The proposed changes also would address the ongoing requirements for Clearing Members. 1. Confidentiality Standards OCC's proposed confidentiality standards apply generally to its membership rules. Proposed Rule 207(d) sets forth the standards Clearing Members must observe when maintaining or exchanging ``OCC Confidential Information'' --the proposed rule demands that members exercise a standard of care that it would employ to protect its own confidential information, but not less than a reasonable standard of care. The proposed rule further acknowledges that breach of confidentiality may result in OCC seeking injunction or other equitable relief against the breaching party and states that the rule does not preclude or otherwise prohibit OCC from providing confidential information to the government or other regulatory authority. 2. Conditions for Admission OCC proposes several changes to its Clearing Membership eligibility and admission standards, which are generally set forth in Chapter II of its rules. First, proposed rule 201(b) requires Clearing Members or applicants to maintain an operating history of at least one year in the same or substantially same business activities the member or applicant applies for. Alternatively, the member or applicant can maintain senior personnel with sufficient background or experience in such business activities. Rule 204 sets forth OCC's Conditions to Admission. OCC proposes to amend its rules with regard to who is authorized to approve or deny applications for Clearing Membership. In 2016, OCC vested authority to approve or disapprove new membership applications in the risk committee of its board of directors (the ``Risk Committee'') and delegated authority to approve certain applications to specific members of OCC management. Now, OCC proposes to allow the Risk Committee to delegate, to its designated delegates or agents, the ability to approve or deny new applications or reapplications. Specifically, OCC proposes amending Rules 203(b) through (e), Rule 204(a), (c) through (e), and (l) to include the phrase ``or its designated delegates or agents,'' which would vest in OCC's management the Risk Committee's authority to approve or deny certain applications and reapplications for Clearing Membership and requests for business expansion. OCC states that the purpose of permitting such delegation is streamline and accelerate the decision-making process and approval, while continuing to utilize a risk-based decision-making approach. OCC states further that the change would eliminate the need to wait until scheduled quarterly Risk Committee meetings to determine whether it will approve such applications or business expansion requests. The proposed changes would also amend an applicant's obligations to notify OCC regarding Statutory Disqualification. Specifically, OCC proposes to require that such notifications be provided not only where an applicant or Key Person is subject to a Statutory Disqualification, but also where the applicant or person is subject to formal investigation by a regulatory organization. OCC proposes to require that such notice be provided within two business days. OCC next proposes amending Chapter II to include new Rules 204(e), (f) and (g). Rule 204(e) would set forth the standards by which OCC may disapprove an application or reapplication for membership or otherwise restrict denied applicants from reapplying upon becoming aware of any facts or circumstances about said applicant or reapplicant that poses elevated risk to OCC or otherwise impacts the suitability of the applicant as a Clearing Member. Self-Regulatory Organizations; Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Its Fee Schedule To Update the Definition of Trading Platform

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend the definition of ``Trading Platform'' set forth in the Definitions section of its Fee Schedule. The existing definition enumerates three categories of execution venue--registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, and an Electronic Communications Network. The Exchange now seeks to amend this definition to add a functional, use-based category--namely, any other system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity--so that the term also captures other systems that perform a functionally equivalent execution function. The amended definition identifies, as non-exhaustive examples, a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment. The current and proposed amended definitions are set forth below. Current Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), or an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS).'' Proposed Amended Definition: ``A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS), or any other system, facility, or platform (including but not limited to a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, or a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment) through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity.'' The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, including the increasing use of functionally equivalent execution systems that operate outside the three enumerated categories. For example, under the current definition, a platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, or an Electronic Communications Network plainly constitutes a Trading Platform and is thus subject to the applicable fees associated with a Trading Platform. However, a functionally equivalent system that performs the same execution function--such as a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow, or a decentralized or tokenized execution venue--is not expressly named in the current enumerated categories, despite performing the same execution function as the enumerated venues. To facilitate more consistent and equitable outcomes across functionally equivalent venues, the Exchange proposes to add this language so that ``Trading Platform'' better covers the intended scope of execution venues. The new framework operates as a functional, use-based standard. It reaches any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of the execution model employed. The definition expressly covers both (i) systems that match third-party orders against one another and (ii) systems in which the operator or its affiliate executes third-party orders in a principal trading capacity. Accordingly, a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/ or facilitates execution of client order flow falls within the definition on its face. The parenthetical examples--a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment--are illustrative only and the amended definition is not intended to limit the scope of the broader category. The requirement that orders be ``systematically executed by electronic means'' distinguishes covered systems from manual, negotiated, or voice-brokered bilateral trading. The amended definition is intended to capture emerging technologies and execution venues that are functionally analogous to venues with established regulatory definitions--including tokenized order books or decentralized execution protocols, to the extent they perform or support an execution function, and other novel platforms. These venues operate in a manner similar to defined legacy execution platforms and should be treated as such. The examples set out in the definition-- broker crossing systems not filed as ATSs, systematic internalization systems, and decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environments-- as well as the references to single-dealer platforms in this filing, are illustrative of this approach, not an exhaustive list, and the definition applies to any system through which third-party orders are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of label. The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity as to the scope of ``Trading Platform,'' with new and emerging execution technologies in mind. The Exchange notes that this update better aligns itself with the ongoing evolution of market structure and industry practice. 2.
